assessments.technical_explanation: The stable-release pipeline forwards every repository secret to the reusable Android build workflow in the same repository. The Android signing secrets match the signing and upload steps that publish builds, but blanket inheritance also exposes unrelated secrets to that job. The workflow starts only from a stable-version tag push or manual dispatch, both of which require write access, so no attacker-controlled trigger or untrusted data flow is demonstrated.
assessments.layman_explanation: When a stable release is built, the Android job receives every stored secret rather than just the Android signing ones. Only maintainers can push release tags or start the run, so this is over-sharing within a trusted pipeline.
assessments.developer_action: Pass only the Android signing secrets explicitly to the called workflow.

assessments.technical_explanation: The orchestrating CI workflow forwards the repository's entire secret set to the reusable Android build workflow. That build legitimately needs the Android signing material even in cache-warming runs because artifacts are deliberately signed, but blanket inheritance also hands over secrets the Android leg never uses. Triggers are restricted to a weekly schedule, filtered pushes to the default branch, and manual dispatch, all of which require write access, so no attacker-controlled trigger path is demonstrated.
assessments.layman_explanation: The main build pipeline hands every stored secret to the Android build job even though that job only needs the Android signing secrets. Only maintainers can start these builds, so this is a tidiness issue rather than a live danger.
assessments.developer_action: Replace blanket secret inheritance with explicit forwarding of only the Android signing secrets the called workflow actually consumes.

assessments.technical_explanation: The release-body input uses logical operators to emulate a conditional. Because the intended empty-string branch is falsy in the workflow expression language, the fallback text is selected in every case, including re-runs where an existing draft already contains hand-edited notes. The documented intent of preserving typed notes on re-run therefore fails, and those notes can be overwritten. This is a self-inflicted automation correctness defect with recoverable loss of typed text; there is no attacker-controlled path, secret exposure, or user-facing harm demonstrated.
assessments.layman_explanation: A clever one-line shortcut meant to leave release notes alone on a re-run does not actually work: the default note text always wins, so any notes a maintainer typed into the draft can be replaced. It is an annoying bug in the release script, not a security hole.
assessments.developer_action: Compute the release body in a preceding script step that emits an empty value on re-run, or gate the input with a genuine conditional, and verify the re-run scenario with a test.

assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged constant is a fallback bearer token for a third-party character-search API used by the discovery feature. The surrounding code shows the primary path fetches this same token by scraping the provider's public client-side configuration script, which the provider serves to every browser visitor, so the constant is a public client identifier rather than a private project credential. It authorizes only search queries against that third-party service, is unrelated to this application's users, their stories, or their model-provider keys, and no concrete harm to users is demonstrated. The residual issues are hygiene: a secret-shaped literal in source that trips scanners, potential reliance on a token the provider can rotate, and downstream host allow-listing that appropriately constrains fetched content.
assessments.layman_explanation: The flagged string is a search key for a public character-directory website, the same key that website hands to every visitor's browser. It is not the app's own password and cannot reach anything belonging to the user; it just looks like a leaked secret to scanning tools.
assessments.developer_action: Document the value as a public client token with a scanner allowlist annotation, and prefer shipping only the dynamic token-fetch path so provider rotation degrades gracefully instead of depending on a stale constant.

assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged step uses a popular third-party release action to create a draft release and attach the built artifact. The audit rule notes that the hosted runner's built-in command-line tooling can already do this, so the action is an avoidable supply-chain dependency. The reusable workflow is invoked only from tag-triggered or default-branch pipelines under maintainer control, and the supplied evidence shows no untrusted trigger, no exfiltration, and no obfuscation. The finding is release-automation hygiene, not demonstrated exposure.
assessments.layman_explanation: The build recipe borrows a community helper tool to publish releases when GitHub's own built-in tools could do the same job. Relying on fewer outside helpers slightly shrinks the surface for a compromised helper to misuse the pipeline, but nothing here shows any actual harm.
assessments.developer_action: Prefer the runner's native release commands for draft creation and asset upload, or if the action is kept, pin it to a full commit hash rather than a floating major tag.

assessments.technical_explanation: The draft-creation step uses a third-party release action although the runner's built-in command-line tooling provides equivalent functionality. This is an avoidable external dependency in a pipeline that holds write access and signing material. The workflow triggers only on version tags or manual dispatch under maintainer control, and the supplied evidence shows no exfiltration or untrusted input, so the finding is supply-chain hygiene rather than demonstrated exposure.
assessments.layman_explanation: The release pipeline uses an outside helper for a job GitHub's own tools can already do. Cutting outside helpers reduces the fallout if that helper were ever compromised, but nothing here indicates any problem today.
assessments.developer_action: Use the runner's native release commands, or pin the action to a full commit hash instead of a floating tag.

assessments.technical_explanation: The pre-release pipeline forwards all repository secrets to the reusable desktop build workflow in the same repository. Only the desktop packaging or signing material is proportionate to that job's steps. Triggering requires pushing a version tag or manual dispatch, both write-access operations, so the over-sharing is confined to maintainer-initiated runs and no attacker-controlled activation or untrusted data flow is demonstrated.
assessments.layman_explanation: The desktop build job for pre-releases also receives every stored secret when only a few are relevant. Only maintainers can start it, so this is over-sharing inside a trusted pipeline.
assessments.developer_action: Forward only the desktop-build secrets the called workflow needs instead of inheriting the full set.

assessments.technical_explanation: The release-body input emulates a conditional with logical operators. Because the intended empty-string branch is falsy in the workflow expression language, the fallback body text is chosen in every run, including re-runs against an existing draft whose notes were typed by hand. The stated intent of preserving those notes therefore fails, and the loss is limited to overwritten draft text. No attacker-controlled path, secret exposure, or user-facing harm is demonstrated; this is an automation correctness defect.
assessments.layman_explanation: A one-line shortcut meant to keep existing release notes on a re-run always picks the default note instead, so notes typed into a draft can be overwritten. It is a scripting bug, not a security hole.
assessments.developer_action: Set the body from a preceding script step that emits an empty value on re-run, or use a real conditional, and test the re-run path.
